content: Deceleration of diastolic flow refers to the slowing down of blood flow during the diastolic phase of the cardiac cycle. The deceleration time of diastolic flow velocity (DDT) is a measurable parameter that can be used to assess the extent of microvascular damage. This parameter may also serve as a predictor of residual myocardial viability, as determined through angiographic studies. Deceleration is defined as the slowing of dye flow within an artery at any point during its course. The diastolic deceleration rate, expressed in meters per second squared (m/s²), quantifies the rate at which flow velocity decreases during diastole. Microvascular ischemic damage, which occurs following occlusion of an epicardial coronary artery, alters coronary vascular resistance. This damage can lead to perivascular edema and the formation of capillary leukocyte plugs, which impede the full restoration of myocardial perfusion. Consequently, the deceleration time of diastolic flow velocity reflects an increase in coronary vascular resistance caused by ischemic microvascular impairment. This phenomenon significantly impacts total coronary resistance, even in patients without severe coronary stenosis. The reduction in post-procedural coronary systolic flow velocity observed in patients with no-reflow is explained by this increase in coronary vascular resistance. Similarly, this mechanism accounts for the marked rise in total coronary resistance in patients without significant coronary stenosis. The deceleration time of diastolic flow velocity may serve as an indicator of coronary blood flow and is associated with a high ratio of perfused myocardium to functioning coronary microvasculature. The degree of reduced systolic antegrade flow or the deceleration time of diastolic flow provides evidence of the extent of microvascular damage and may predict residual myocardial viability. In viable myocardium, coronary blood flow velocity patterns appear nearly normal. However, in nonviable myocardium, these patterns are diminished due to systolic retrograde flow and rapid deceleration of diastolic flow velocity. In terms of clinical significance, the coronary blood flow velocity pattern in patients with no-reflow following reperfused acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is characterized by the following features: Systolic retrograde flow. Reduced systolic antegrade flow. Rapid deceleration of diastolic flow. These abnormalities may occur immediately after reperfusion or shortly thereafter. Additionally, disturbances during the deceleration phase of systole are observed in cases of mild to moderate coronary stenosis.
